# Preface.

I undertake to reveal the life and fortunes, the subtle schemes, and the deceptions of a man who, in more than one respect, belongs among the remarkable phenomena of our age.

No fraudster of modern times went so far, possessed such well-thought-out plans, or employed as much cunning and craftiness in their execution as the notorious Franz Matthäus Grossinger. Boundless imagination, untamed pride, groveling falsehood, Jesuitical cunning <note>Historically, the term "Jesuitical" was used as a pejorative to describe someone perceived as being deceptive, manipulative, or using complex logic to justify dishonest acts.</note>, insolent audacity, excessive egoism, and a boundless inclination toward soft living and sordid extravagance

What else could be expected from a man of this sort than schemes and base acts; what else than the employment of every means—no matter how little they aligned with justice and goodness—if only his ignoble ends could be achieved?

Grossinger was not poorly educated; he dressed with more neatness than splendor; his manners were so polished through social interaction that he could adapt, bend, and shape himself to any situation. Through certain secret hints of grandeur—which appeared to be dropped entirely without intent—he often knew how to give himself such an air of importance that even men with vast experience of the world were misled by him. They could not bring themselves to believe that malice could so skillfully wrap itself in the **cloak of virtue** <note>The original German "Tugendmantel" refers to a metaphorical cloak used to hide one's true, often wicked, intentions under a display of morality.</note> or know how to hide behind the mask of unrecognized and slighted merit.

The honest German was not yet accustomed to such language; people believed that a man who speaks as Grossinger does is either innocent, or if he is not entirely so, then such important things must have happened to him that he is allowed to chatter and shout so unpunished.

# Grossings

## Life and Adventures.

Franz Rudolph von Grossing was the son of a <term>middle-class</term> <note>German: *bürgerlich*. This indicates that while he was not of noble birth, his family held a respected status within the town's social hierarchy.</note> <term>master butcher</term> <note>German: *Fleischhackermeister*.</note> in Komárno, Hungary, and was born in 1752. His father, Franz Grossinger, is still living at this moment and is currently a <term>councilman</term> <note>German: *Rathsmann*.</note> in the <term>free city</term> <note>A city that held specific royal privileges and a degree of self-governance.</note> of Komárno. One will be all the less surprised that a master butcher can be a councilman, as it is quite common in several German cities for craftsmen to hold positions in the <term>magistracy</term> <note>The governing body of a city.</note>.

### Grossing's
# Life and Adventures.

Franz Rudolph von Grossing was the son of a middle-class master butcher in Komárom <note>German: *Comorn*. A significant fortified city on the Danube, then part of the Kingdom of Hungary.</note> in Hungary, and was born in 1752. His father, Franz Grossinger, is still living at this very moment and is currently a councilman <term>Rathsmann: A member of the local municipal council or a magistrate.</term> in the free city of Komárom. One will be all the less surprised that a master butcher can be a councilman, as it is quite common in several German cities for craftsmen to hold magisterial positions. 

Besides the hero of our story, he had two other sons: namely, one named Joseph, who is employed by the Police College <note>German: *Polizeicollegio*. This refers to the administrative and judicial body governing the police in 18th-century Vienna.</note> in Vienna, and another named Ignatz, who resides near Szombathely <note>German: *Stein am Anger*. A historic city in western Hungary near the Austrian border.</note> and is said to make his living from the cattle trade <term>Ochsenhandel: Literally "ox trade," a significant economic activity in Hungary at the time.</term>. In addition, he had four daughters, of whom the eldest [was married] to the Apos

thecary Weinpassinger in Kőszeg <note>German: *Günz*. A town in western Hungary.</note>, and the other is married to the city legal advisor <term>Stadtsyndikus: A senior legal officer or magistrate representing a city's interests.</term> Joseph Strahler in Komárom <note>German: *Comorn*.</note>. That the name of our adventurer <note>German: *Abentheurer*. In the 18th century, this often carried a negative connotation of a swindler or social climber.</note> must therefore be borrowed goes without saying; for it is ever the trait of small souls to be ashamed of their parents and other relatives, though for the most part, it is only the parents who have cause for shame. His actual baptismal name is Franz Matthäus Grossing or Grossinger. For the "(er)" is an addition that his father had already adopted. The mother of our hero was named Rosalia Dobies and was the daughter of a tanner <term>Gerber: A leather maker or tanner.</term> born in Pest <note>Now the eastern half of Budapest, Hungary.</note>. One sees, therefore, that our man’s nobility, and even more so his claim to being a Baron, stood on very weak legs, and was founded on nothing but his boundless, ridiculous pride. For his grandfather—to whom he refers on so many occasions and who, as he claimed, was supposedly a nobleman from Bavaria and commander of the fortress of Győr <note>German: *Raab*. A major city in northwest Hungary.</note>—was merely a dragoon <term>Dragoner: A type of cavalry soldier who traditionally fought as mounted infantry.</term> in the Imperial service. Born in Königsbrunn and named Christian Grossing, he became a master butcher <term>Fleischhackermeister: A master of the butchers' guild.</term> and cattle trader in Komárom after leaving the military.

->Question 1. What is the actual name of the man calling<-
->himself Franz Rudolph von Grossing?<-

Answer. To Question 1. I live in the immediate neighborhood of the current Senator, Mr. Franz Grossinger, whose children I know well, specifically the Franz Grossinger in question; however, I do not know if he is also named Rudolph. It could be that he adopted the name Rudolph from his confirmation <note>Original: *Fermung*, a variant of *Firmung*. In the Catholic tradition, it is common to choose a new saint's name during the sacrament of Confirmation.</note>.

->Question 2. Whether he is of the nobility?<-

To Question 2. That is unknown to me, and even the father, Senator Franz Grossinger, is not treated as noble by the Free City of Komárom <note>Original: *Comorn*. A historic city on the Danube, now divided between Hungary and Slovakia.</note>, as I recall that he never claimed this prerogative <term>Prerogative: Here referring to the legal rights, tax exemptions, and social status reserved for the nobility.</term> for himself.

->Question 3. Who was his father, and whether he is alive?<-

To Question 3. His father is named Franz Grossinger; he is still living today and is a councilman <term>Rathsmann: A member of the municipal council; a civic official.</term> of the Free City of Komárom. By trade, however, he is a butcher <term>Fleischhacker: An archaic German term for a butcher.</term>, which trade he practiced here in Komárom as a master for a long time.

Let us now proceed further with his life story.

The father, a man of some means, sent his sons to the local Jesuit college <term>Collegium: a secondary school or higher institution run by the Jesuit Order</term>, where most of the town's children received their early schooling. He intended to dedicate his two eldest sons—whose talent for study was unmistakable—to the monastic life.

To bring this about, Joseph and Franz (the elder brother and our hero) were sent to Ofen <note>Ofen is the German name for Buda, the hilly part of modern-day Budapest</note>, where the "sons of Loyola" <note>A reference to the Society of Jesus (Jesuits), founded by Ignatius of Loyola</note> had established a college and a seminary. In no other realm—not even Spain—did this Society enjoy such high regard, nor was it perhaps as widespread as it was in Hungary, where every town, even the small ones, possessed a seminary or at least a monastery and a college.

This Order, which at that time managed almost all school education and thus exerted such great influence over both the high-born and the lowly, was very eager to recruit pupils, and even worked in secret to do so. And how could it, with its almost un- <note>The text here breaks off, continuing on the next page with the word "limited" (begränzten)</note>

From the former, Father Porters or Cellar Masters <note>The "Pater Pförtner" (Porter) and "Kellermeister" (Cellarer) were administrative or domestic roles, often given to those with practical skills or family wealth rather than academic brilliance.</note> were fashioned; from the latter, Father Rectors.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Franz Rudolph Grossing's dual identity as "Madame von Rosenwald." It explains how his arrogance and administrative chaos led him to keep incriminating documents that proved his fraudulent activities in Hungary.</meta>

Since he himself was a wretched hybrid <note>The German "Mittelding" (middle-thing/hybrid) refers to Grossing’s performance of dual identities—a man acting as a woman—rather than a biological description.</note> between man and woman, representing in a single person both the **Madame von Rosenwald** and the notorious ex-Jesuit **Franz Rudolph Grossinger**, the reports of his own life naturally had to come to his attention. <meta>This page provides the official text of the legal pledge signed by Franz Rudolph Grossing, whose physical description was detailed on the previous page. While page 67 was a public notice for his arrest should he return, this page records the specific "Bond of Non-Return" he signed on February 3, 1783, prior to his escorted expulsion to the Hungarian border.</meta>

<page-num>( 68 )</page-num>

->Here is the *Bond of Non-Return.* <note>original: *Revers de non redeundo*; a formal legal pledge signed by a person being banished, promising never to return to the territory on pain of harsher punishment</note><-

Since I, *Franz Rudolph Grossing*, have been taken into custody by the local Imperial-Royal City and Provincial Court due to the crime of clipping ducats <note>German: *Dukatenbeschneidung*; the illegal practice of shaving small amounts of metal from the edges of gold coins to sell the shavings while still attempting to spend the diminished coin at face value</note> attributed to me, and legal proceedings have been conducted against me such that—according to the investigation carried out and the decree issued by a Most Honorable Imperial-Royal Court of Appeals regarding my completed arrest—I am to be banished from all Imperial-Royal German Hereditary Lands <note>the core territories of the Habsburg Empire, including modern-day Austria and parts of Germany and Czechia</note> upon the submission of a *Bond of Non-Return*, and consequently shall be immediately escorted by the guard to the Hungarian border.

Therefore, by virtue of this present bond, I vow, declare, and promise that for the duration of my life I will not, nor shall I, allow myself to be found within the Imperial-Royal German Hereditary Lands again; otherwise, should I act to the contrary, I shall be proceeded against with full severity as a defiant violator of exile <note>German: *frevelhaften Revertenten*; one who wickedly or audaciously returns despite a legal ban</note> in accordance with the High Sovereign Decree.

In witness whereof, I have left this completed bond with the local Imperial-Royal City and Provincial Court. *Vienna*, the 3rd of *February* 1783.

The reviewer in the *General Literature Gazette* <note>original: "Allgemeinen Litteratur-Zeitung," one of the most important German-language literary periodicals of the late 18th century</note> concludes his review with the following words:

> "Will not every honorable father and

> reading it, to see justice done to the little book
> upon his own household hearth?" <note>This is a polite contemporary suggestion that the book is so offensive or worthless that it should be burned immediately.</note>

He <note>the reviewer</note> foresees in his mind that these violent outbursts of nonsense might be restrained not in chains and bonds—as Grossing himself already believed at the time—but rather in a madhouse.

Our hero’s gift of foresight must have been stronger than that of the reviewer, since his prognosis <term>prognosis; a forecast of the likely course of a disease or situation, here used to describe a prediction of one's fate</term> came to pass so accurately and so definitely. Regarding No. 846. This petition having been read through, the present Lord Ordinary Magistrate Fiscal <note>original: "Magistratualis Fiscalis"; a legal official who acted as a public prosecutor or state attorney for the county</note>, **Ignatius Gerdenich**, verbally protested against the fact that the aforementioned **Grossinger** had dared to present himself as a Noble of the Kingdom of Hungary, since he was never included in the List of Nobles of this County, nor has he ever lived as a member of the nobility.

Furthermore, since the burden of proof for the claimed nobility would lie with the said **Grossinger** as the one making the claim, it would be unusual—and indeed, hardly consistent with the principles of humanity—to issue authentic testimonial letters regarding the fact that he is *not* a Noble. To do so would be to issue a document based on a "negative proposition" of the broadest kind. This is especially true for a man who is not subject to this county's jurisdiction, but was born to a father who was a Senator and Citizen of Komárom <note>original: "Comaroniensi"; the Latin name for the city of Komárom. Moreover, it was resolved that authentic Testimonial Letters should be issued regarding this official recording <term>Protocollation</term> (the formal entry of these proceedings into the record) alone. Based on this recording, we have deemed it necessary and just to grant and issue these, our present authentic Testimonial Letters, secured with the Seal of our County, as common justice requires.

Love of truth—well, if that is so, then the author of his life story deserves all the respect and friendship of which one is capable, since he has made truth the primary duty in the composition of his autobiography. The great driving force of the entire <term>Order of the Rosy Cross<note>German: *Rosenorden*; referring here to the 18th-century Gold and Rosy Cross, a quasi-masonic secret society that claimed ancient mystical origins but was often accused of political and financial manipulation.</note> was Grossing's private purse: it was this that distributed patents, medals, seals, and robes like a <term>Pantalone<note>German: *Pantalon*; a character from the Italian *Commedia dell'arte* representing a wealthy, sometimes foolish or miserly merchant. Here, the author uses it to describe someone handing out titles and costumes as if they were theatrical props.</note>; he was the inventor of the secrets of an Order that is ridiculous in itself, and has nothing mysterious about it other than its language.

The progenitor of the Order of the Rosy Cross was hunger and despair—its cradle, cunning and intrigue—its youth, shameful, concealed <term>money-grubbing<note>German: *Geldschneiderei*; specifically refers to the exploitative practice of swindling people out of their money, often through inflated fees or false promises.</note> wrapped in the cloak of virtue—its manhood, blatant fraud and villainy—and now, bent over a staff and burdened with heavy chains, it creeps toward the grave along with its great founder. The entire span of its life lasted five to six years—

# The Grand Mastership.

Although the Foundress-Rose <note>original: *Stiftsrose*; referring to the central or founding chapter/authority of the Order</note> is the actual head of the Order, there nonetheless exists within it another dignity besides this one: namely, the Grand Mastership. This Grand Mastership is the highest honorary position and consists of a Grand Mistress and a Grand Master. All complaints that an individual member, a local rose <note>original: *Localrose*; a local branch or chapter</note>, or a national rose <note>original: *Nationalrose*; a regional governing body</note> might have against the Foundress fall under the jurisdiction of the Grand Mastership. This Grand Mastership is therefore, in a sense, the mediator or the focal point between the head of the institution and its subordinates; it represents the entire Order at all public appearances, so that while the Grand Mistress and Grand Master constitute the highest-ranking persons, they remain—as members of a local rose—subordinate to the Foundress-Rose as the general head.

By this law, he surrendered nothing; for what he sacrificed with one hand, he took back with the other.

In these matters, Grossing required all possible cunning, for the demands of the ladies and gentlemen of the Rose often became so vehement that he knew not how to help himself or what counsel to take. On such occasions, he usually dismissed these persons from the Order; or, if their demands had been too impetuous—that is, if they had told him the bitter truth to his face, that he was leading a shameful life with the money intended for the poor—such a member might even be expelled from the Order. This expulsion always presupposed an offense against honor and conscience <note>Grossing would claim the member had committed a moral failing to justify the expulsion, thereby protecting his own reputation while silencing critics.</note>.

### Method of Admission

Whoever desires to be admitted into the Rose Institute either already knows a member of the same, or he does not yet know one. If he knows one, he simply has to turn to that person, and then receives further instruction from them.

### Voluntary Resignation.

The Rose Institute is subject to no compulsion. Therefore, every member is free to resign at all times; however, to maintain order, permission must first be obtained from the Chapter Rose <term>Stiftsrose; the governing "Mother Lodge" or central authority of the order</term>, including a statement of the underlying reasons, and a sworn bond <term>eidlicher Revers; a formal written commitment or legal pledge made under oath</term> directed toward the observance of eternal secrecy must be issued. Anyone who receives their resignation in this manner is considered honorably discharged; otherwise, they are regarded as expelled.

Why the need for a double sworn bond for a matter which, as he himself says, has no secrets; for a matter that aims for the well-being of humanity? — —

## Forced Expulsion.

Members who make themselves unworthy of the Institute by violating that which they entered into by pledging their honor and conscience can no longer be tolerated within it. If any such member is found, a report is made to the Chapter Rose <term>Stiftsrose; the central governing authority or "Mother Lodge" of the order</term>, which then—after an investigation has been conducted and the truth proven—is solely authorized to decree the expulsion. Between these two types of departure <note>meaning voluntary resignation versus forced expulsion</note> there exists a great difference. For situation and circumstances can sometimes compel a member against their will to leave the Rose Covenant <note>original: "Rosenbunde"; the fraternity or alliance of the Rosicrucians</note>; therefore, a discharge is not dishonorable; furthermore, the discharged individual always retains the freedom to apply for re-admission. However, since expulsion always presupposes a crime committed against honor and conscience, no expelled person can ever be admitted to the Rose Covenant again.

### Persistence of Their Duties.

Neither through dismissal nor through expulsion do the duties cease which a member entered into upon joining; and whoever possesses honor and conscience will never violate these, since the pledged honor and conscience is the greatest oath for honor-loving people. Every member is obliged to observe the same secrecy toward dismissed and expelled individuals regarding all affairs of the Institute as they would toward complete strangers.

Grossing <note>Franz Rudolf von Grossing (1752–1789), a prolific adventurer and founder of various secret societies, including the Rose Order described here.</note> was reluctant to grant dismissals and used every possible means—employing all manner of cunning—to thwart them. If, however, a member stubbornly insisted upon leaving, such members were preferred to be formally expelled to avoid setting a "bad example." For he was quite certain that no dismissed person would ever re-enter the Order. As proof of all this, I need only cite the <term>Silesian Rose</term> <note>original: "Schlesische Rose"; a specific branch or "lodge" of the order located in Silesia.</note>, where the dismissal and expulsion certificates were dated from Dresden and [signed] with Frau von Rosenwald's name under- <note>The text ends mid-word on the catchword "unter-", likely completing as "unterschrieben" (signed) on the following page.</note>

### Duty in Regard to Children.

Every member blessed with children of the Rose Institute <note>original: "Roseninstitut"</note> is obligated to educate these children from their earliest childhood to be future members of the Order; for indeed, no specific age is determined for admission.

One sees that Grossing <note>Franz Rudolf von Grossing, the order's founder.</note> even provided for posterity; even children were meant to have the great fortune of being members of the Rose.

->Imperial Count of F. . . 1788.<-

A counterfeit coin, whose composition one knows because one has often been cheated by it, attracts attention. One becomes suspicious of all similar imprints, and rightly so. One does not take them blindly, on faith and credit, but rather examines and compares them. So it was with me regarding this book; how could I fail to immediately discover the source that so easily betrayed itself?

The whole thing bore too much the stamp of Grossing’s characteristic adventurousness <term>Abentheuerlichkeit: This refers to the flamboyant and reckless charlatanry typical of 18th-century "adventurers" or con artists like Grossing.</term> for me to believe even for a moment that the Imperial Count of F... <note>Likely referring again to Count Fugger-Hoheneck, who acted as a patron to Grossing.</note>, whom I knew from his *Letters of the Rose* <note>Rosenbriefe: These were publications or manifestos associated with the "Order of the Rose," a pseudo-chivalric secret society Grossing used to exploit the nobility.</note> to be a very noble man, was supposed to be the author (which, in this case, is the same as being the translator). This suspicion became a certainty when I read the following passage in the preface:

> "This work (the *Harmony*) is of such important content that it [should be] translated into all the vernacular languages of the world, and by everyone who [seeks] his own and his fellow men's happiness at the—"

<summary>The author explains why he immediately recognized the book "Harmony" as a fraud written by Grossing, despite it being officially attributed to the Imperial Count of F.
